title: How much HIIT?
goal: Plan how many interval sessions to do, of what size, spread or in blocks, and recognise when too much HIIT turns into non-functional overreaching.

steps.title: How much of the week?
steps.text:
Logs of national and international endurance athletes training 10–13 times a week converge on one pattern: about **80%** of sessions at low intensity, and about **20%** built around hard work such as intervals near 90% of VO₂max [[c:seiler-8020]]. In a [polarised](g:polarised-training) week, HIIT is that hard 20%. For 10 sessions a week, that's about 2 interval sessions.

Is more HIIT better for athletes who are already well trained? Studies that added more of it haven't given convincing proof of long-term gains [[c:seiler-intensify]]. An earlier review argued the other way: once trained, gains come only from HIIT. Both can hold at once: HIIT may be needed, yet more of it may not help.

claims.text: Elite endurance athletes do about 80% of sessions at low intensity and about 20% with high-intensity work, such as intervals near 90% of VO₂max.

evidence.quote: about 80% of training sessions are performed at low intensity (2 mM blood lactate), with about 20% dominated by periods of high-intensity work, such as interval training at approx. 90% VO2max

claims.text: Training intensification studies in well-trained athletes give no convincing evidence that more HIIT brings long-term performance gains.

evidence.quote: Training intensification studies performed on already well-trained athletes do not provide any convincing evidence that a greater emphasis on high-intensity interval training in this highly trained athlete population gives long-term performance gains.

debate.question: Do already well-trained athletes gain from adding more HIIT?

sides.position: Yes, in a sense: in highly trained athletes, extra easy volume adds little, and further gains seem to come only through HIIT.
Not clearly: intensification studies give no convincing evidence of long-term gains, and elite athletes settle on about 20% hard sessions.

steps.title: How much per session, for how many weeks?
steps.text:
A meta-analysis of 53 RCTs sorted HIIT protocols by their VO₂max effect. The largest effects came with long work intervals (**≥ 2 min**), **≥ 15 min** of work per session, and **4–12 weeks** or more. Short (≤ 30 s), low-volume (≤ 5 min of work) and short-term (≤ 4 weeks) HIIT still worked, above all in the general population [[c:wen-protocol]].

For performance, a meta-analysis of 29 studies found that time-trial gains rose with the number of HIIT sessions, weeks and total work, but not with SIT. Its authors add that going beyond the minimum dose may not add much [[c:rosenblat-dose]].

So dose matters, up to a point.

claims.text: HIIT with long intervals (≥2 min), high volume (≥15 min of work) and 4–12 weeks or more gave the largest VO₂max effects; short, low-volume, short-term HIIT is also effective, especially in the general population.

evidence.quote: To maximize the training effects on VO2max, long-interval (≥2min), high-volume (≥15min) and moderate to long-term (≥4-12weeks) HIIT are recommended.
Short-intervals (≤30s), low-volume (≤5min) and short-term (≤4weeks) HIIT represent effective and time-efficient strategies for developing VO2max, especially for the general population.

claims.text: Time-trial gains showed a dose–response with HIIT sessions, weeks and total work, but not with SIT; more than the minimum dose may not add to the response.

evidence.quote: There was a dose-response relationship with the number of HIIT sessions, training weeks and total work with changes in TT performance. However, the dose-response was not present with SIT.
Our analysis suggests that increasing interval training dose beyond minimal requirements may not augment the training response.

steps.title: Spread it out, or pack it in?
steps.text:
[Block periodisation](g:block-periodisation) packs hard sessions together. Nineteen trained cyclists trained for 4 weeks [[c:block-ronn]]:

| | week 1 | weeks 2–4 |
|---|---|---|
| block | 5 HIIT sessions | 1 HIIT session a week |
| traditional | 2 HIIT sessions | 2 HIIT sessions a week |

Both groups did the same total HIIT and easy volume. The block group raised VO₂max by 4.6% and peak power by 2.1%; the traditional group didn't change.

A hard [microcycle](g:microcycle) like week 1 is meant to tire you: its gains show up after the easy days that follow. One small trial, not randomised, over 4 weeks: promising, not settled.

claims.text: In trained cyclists, a block of 5 HIIT sessions in week 1 then 1 a week raised VO₂max, peak power and power at 2 mmol·L⁻¹ lactate, while 2 sessions a week for 4 weeks didn't, at the same total volume.

evidence.quote: While BP increased VO2max , peak power output (Wmax) and power output at 2 mmol/L [la(-)] by 4.6 ± 3.7%, 2.1 ± 2.8%, and 10 ± 12%, respectively (P < 0.05), no changes occurred in TRAD.
the first week constituted five sessions of high-intensity aerobic training (HIT), followed by 3 weeks of one weekly HIT session and focus on low-intensity training (LIT)

steps.title: When hard becomes too much
steps.text:
Training needs overload, but not overload plus too little recovery. A short dip after a hard block that turns into a gain after recovery is [functional overreaching](g:functional-overreaching). Ignore the balance and you get [non-functional overreaching](g:nonfunctional-overreaching): a longer dip with no gain. Telling that apart from the [overtraining syndrome](g:overtraining-syndrome) is very hard, and rests on how things turn out and on ruling out other causes [[c:meeusen-or]].

The body shows it too. When volunteers' training load was raised step by step over 4 weeks, the heaviest week cut their mitochondrial function and disturbed blood glucose control [[c:flockhart]].

So a HIIT block is a planned overreach: plan the easy days after it as carefully as the block.

claims.text: Functional overreaching leads to better performance after recovery; without enough recovery, non-functional overreaching can occur, and telling it from overtraining syndrome is very difficult.

evidence.quote: This functional overreaching will eventually lead to an improvement in performance after recovery.
When athletes do not sufficiently respect the balance between training and recovery, nonfunctional overreaching (NFOR) can occur.
The distinction between NFOR and overtraining syndrome (OTS) is very difficult and will depend on the clinical outcome and exclusion diagnosis.

claims.text: After the week with the highest load in a 4-week plan of rising load, mitochondrial function fell sharply and glucose tolerance was disturbed.

evidence.quote: Following the week with the highest exercise load, we found a striking reduction in intrinsic mitochondrial function that coincided with a disturbance in glucose tolerance and insulin secretion.

points: Elite endurance athletes do about 20% of sessions with hard work such as intervals; for most weeks that means 1–3 HIIT sessions.
Whether more HIIT helps trained athletes is debated: it may be needed, yet adding more hasn't clearly paid off.
The largest VO₂max effects came from intervals of ≥ 2 min, ≥ 15 min of work per session and 4–12+ weeks; gains rise with dose, but not without limit.
Block periodisation packs HIIT into a short hard microcycle; it beat even spreading in one small trial, and it needs easy days after it.
A short dip that turns into a gain is functional overreaching; a long dip with no gain is non-functional overreaching or worse.

variants.stem: An amateur triathlete trains 10 times a week and wants to copy the elite share of hard sessions. About how many should be interval sessions?

options.text: About 2
options.why: Right: about 20% of sessions have high-intensity work; 20% of 10 is 2.

options.text: About 5
options.why: That would be half of all sessions, far more than the elite pattern of about 20%.

options.text: About 8
options.why: 80% is the share of low-intensity sessions, not hard ones.

options.text: None: amateurs should only train easy
options.why: The elite pattern includes about 20% hard sessions; it isn't all easy.

variants.stem: A well-trained cyclist already does 2 HIIT sessions a week. A forum post says: 'Double it to 4 and you'll keep improving.' What's the best judgement?

options.text: Unproven: more HIIT hasn't clearly given long-term gains
options.why: Right: intensification studies in well-trained athletes give no convincing evidence of long-term gains.

options.text: Proven: trained athletes improve only through HIIT
options.why: An early review argued HIIT is needed once trained, but that doesn't show that more of it keeps working.

options.text: Wrong: HIIT doesn't work in trained athletes
options.why: Interval training does improve trained athletes, by about 2% in time trials.

options.text: Proven: elite athletes do half their sessions as HIIT
options.why: Elite logs show about 20% hard sessions, not half.

variants.stem: According to the 2019 meta-analysis, which session meets both markers of the largest VO₂max effect: work intervals of at least 2 min, and at least 15 min of work in all?

options.text: 5 × 3 min
options.why: Right: 3 min intervals, and 5 × 3 = 15 min of work.

options.text: 3 series of 13 × 30 s
options.why: 19.5 min of work, but 30 s intervals are short intervals, not ≥ 2 min.

options.text: 4 × 3 min
options.why: Long enough intervals, but only 12 min of work in all.

options.text: 6 × 30 s all-out
options.why: Short intervals and only 3 min of work: a low-volume session.

variants.stem: According to the 2019 meta-analysis, which running session meets both markers of the largest VO₂max effect: work intervals of at least 2 min, and at least 15 min of work in all?

options.text: 4 × 4 min
options.why: Right: 4 min intervals, and 4 × 4 = 16 min of work.

options.text: 3 × 4 min
options.why: Long enough intervals, but only 12 min of work in all.

options.text: 2 series of 20 × 30 s
options.why: 20 min of work, but 30 s intervals are short intervals, not ≥ 2 min.

options.text: 8 × 1 min
options.why: 1 min intervals are under 2 min, and there are only 8 min of work.

variants.stem: In the 2021 meta-analysis of interval training and time-trial performance, how did gains relate to dose?

options.text: They rose with HIIT dose, but not with SIT dose
options.why: Right: gains rose with HIIT sessions, weeks and total work; no dose–response was found for SIT.

options.text: They rose with dose for both HIIT and SIT
options.why: The dose–response was not present with SIT.

options.text: They fell as HIIT dose rose
options.why: Gains rose with HIIT dose, though more than the minimum may not add much.

options.text: Dose made no difference at all
options.why: For HIIT, sessions, weeks and total work were all related to gains.

variants.stem: In the block study, one group did 5 HIIT sessions in week 1 then 1 a week; the other did 2 a week for 4 weeks. What was the difference between the groups?

options.text: How the same HIIT was spread over 4 weeks
options.why: Right: both did 8 HIIT sessions (5 + 3 × 1 and 2 × 4) and similar easy volume; only the spread differed.

options.text: The block group did twice as much HIIT
options.why: Count them: 5 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 8 and 2 × 4 = 8 sessions.

options.text: The block group did no easy training
options.why: Weeks 2–4 of the block focused on low-intensity training.

options.text: The traditional group did SIT instead
options.why: Both groups did high-intensity aerobic intervals; only their timing differed.

variants.stem: After a 6-day block of five 30/15 sessions, a cyclist's power is down for a week. After 6 easy days it is better than before the block. Best description?

options.text: Functional overreaching
options.why: Right: a short dip that turns into a gain after recovery is functional overreaching.

options.text: Non-functional overreaching
options.why: NFOR is a longer dip that brings no gain; here power rose above the starting level.

options.text: Overtraining syndrome
options.why: OTS means a drop lasting months; this one passed in about a week.

options.text: Detraining
options.why: Detraining is the loss of fitness from training too little, not a dip after a hard block.

variants.stem: A runner piles HIIT onto every week for 3 months. Her race times have been worse for 6 weeks, she sleeps badly and rest weeks don't help. Best description so far?

options.text: Non-functional overreaching, or worse
options.why: Right: a dip lasting weeks with no rebound points to NFOR; ruling out other causes would decide whether it is overtraining syndrome.

options.text: Functional overreaching
options.why: Functional overreaching rebounds into a gain after a short recovery; hers hasn't.

options.text: Normal tiredness from one hard week
options.why: Six weeks of falling performance is far more than one hard week.

options.text: Detraining
options.why: She is training more, not less; detraining comes from training too little.

variants.stem: A blog cites the 2021 study (load rising for 4 weeks cut mitochondrial function) as proof that HIIT blocks harm cyclists. What most limits that claim?

options.text: One study of healthy volunteers, not trained cyclists
options.why: Right: it is a single mechanistic study in healthy volunteers with a steeply rising load; it doesn't test planned blocks with recovery in athletes.

options.text: Mitochondria have no role in endurance
options.why: Mitochondrial function is central to endurance; that's why the finding matters.

options.text: The study found the load improved everything
options.why: Mitochondrial function fell and glucose tolerance was disturbed after the heaviest week.

options.text: Four weeks is too short for any change
options.why: Changes did show up within the 4 weeks, after the heaviest week.
